title: The best places to see the northern lights across Canada | Travel Insider
excerpt: Did you know 2026 is set to be the biggest year in a decade for aurora borealis spotting? Here's your guide to the northern lights, including where and when you've got the best chance of seeing them and how to photograph them like a pro.
content:
Growing up in Makkovik – a small Inuit community located in the fjord-carved coast of Labrador in eastern Canada – Wayne Broomfield spent winter nights with his head gazing upward at the sky. “When I whistled, the natural neon lights started moving and dancing. We really did believe it would come down and get us, so whoever stayed out the longest was considered the bravest,” he says.

These memories were pivotal in shaping Broomfield’s career as a freelance polar expedition guide and photographer. “That experience made us more aware of our surroundings – the sky, the weather, everything around us. Even after all these years, I still get a feeling in my gut and I can sense when the lights are about to appear.” On a recent expedition in Nunavut – Canada’s northernmost territory – while camping on the sea ice, he told his guests to face east. “They looked up and said, ‘There’s nothing.’ I said, ‘Just wait.’ Within minutes the first ribbons began to form, moving from east to west, until the whole sky was illuminated.”

Broomfield started working as a guide in the early 2000s but the spectacular landscapes he traversed in 2005 on a trip to the Torngat Mountains – traditional Inuit hunting grounds on the far northern tip of Labrador – sparked his love of photography. He describes the mountains as monoliths rising straight out of the sea. “I was in awe. I came home, bought a camera and taught myself how to use it. I’ve been hooked ever since.”

Colour-blind since birth, photography for Broomfield is more about movement and intuition – he often focuses his camera on an empty patch of sky, knowing the light will find it. “While I can’t always tell the pastel shades apart, I think, well, maybe others can’t see them the way I do. If you start to study the lights, you can almost predict where they’ll go next. Everyone’s facing one way but I’m waiting for the moment it shifts.”

He is now preparing to launch his own company to offer private tours throughout Labrador and the Canadian Arctic. Named “Sila in Harmony” – for the Inuktitut word that encompasses weather, spirit and the intelligence of the natural world – it represents a reverence for nature that underpins every aspect of his work.

“I’m not going to cause environmental damage or get people closer to animals. I think back to the old stories – if you treat the place with respect, you’ll be rewarded. I begin every tour with a moment of silence and remind guests: ‘Just feel how lucky you are to be here.’ Sometimes quiet is extremely powerful,” he says.

Wayne Broomfield’s top tips for photographing the Northern Lights

  • Stabilise: Use a phone tripod or rest your phone on something steady.

  • Use night mode/low-light settings:

    • On iPhone: Night mode (available on iPhone 11 and newer) activates automatically in low light. If you want to extend the exposure even more, tap the moon icon in the camera menu and use the slider to extend the exposure time up to 10 seconds.
    • On Samsung Galaxy: A range of models offer a night mode (called Nightography) feature. To activate it, open the camera, swipe to more and tap Night.

  • Turn off the flash: Even the dimmest flash can wash out the colours.

  • Wear gloves: Wear a pair of touchscreen gloves during colder temperatures so you can operate your phone without exposing your fingers.

  • Avoid the temptation to over-edit: Don’t push the saturation too far and let the natural colours shine.

  • View with your eyes and not just through the lens: What the camera catches versus what the eye captures can be totally different. Take lots of pictures but also take the time to look up.

Step into Aurora science in Churchill, Manitoba

false

original

The Aurora isn’t just a beautiful sight – it’s a scientific phenomenon. In northern Canada, Churchill lies directly beneath the Auroral Oval, one of the most active viewing zones on Earth and where the northern lights sweep across the sky up to 300 nights a year. At the Churchill Northern Studies Centre, researchers study how solar storms collide with Earth’s atmosphere, track the patterns of charged particles and log data that helps explain everything from long-term climate shifts to sudden disruptions of satellites. You can be a part of that work, too – join talks with scientists and hear the latest forecasts before venturing into the subarctic night to witness the sky deliver on the theories.

Lazy Bear Expeditions’ Ultimate Northern Lights Solar Science Adventure takes this blend of research and wonder even further. After settling into your room at the rustic Lazy Bear Lodge and enjoying a meal featuring locally sourced organic ingredients at the Lazy Bear Café, you’ll be guided to remote viewing grounds in and around Churchill. Here, free from light pollution and deep in the forest or on a windswept stretch of coast, you’ll take in the display with traditional bannock fry bread warm in your hand. Under the ethereal glow, Indigenous peoples will share stories of the sky that have been passed down for generations.

The natural wonders don’t stop there: one day you might be in a helicopter, scanning the tundra as caribou move in herds and polar bears pace the edge of Hudson Bay. The next, you might be driven in a purpose-built all-terrain tundra vehicle across those same frozen flats.

Churchill Wild’s Hudson Bay Odyssey begins with a short charter flight from Churchill to Nanuk Polar Bear Lodge, a remote wilderness ecolodge set on the wild southern shores of Hudson Bay. From here, daily walking safaris take you safely onto the tundra to watch – and follow – ambling polar bears from a safe distance. At night, staff monitor the skies and gently wake you when the Aurora appears.

Getting there

VIA Rail’s two-day journey from Winnipeg to Churchill rolls north through prairie, boreal forest and tundra at a pace that invites conversation and connection. Sleeper Plus Class options range from a berth with two stacked beds to cabins with private washrooms that can accommodate three passengers. In the dining car you might share a table with fellow explorers or First Nations Cree and Dene families travelling between communities. By the time you arrive, you’ve already stepped into the region’s subarctic rhythm – especially if you’ve managed to catch a show of northern lights from the train’s glass-topped observation carriage.

Fly into the remote wilderness of the Northwest Territories

false

original

In Yellowknife, the Northern Lights are so bright and best appreciated when you’re surrounded by a vast expanse of forest, tundra and frozen lakes , so you’ll probably want to venture further into the wilderness.

Board a private bush plane for a 20-minute flight over white-blanketed wilderness to Blachford Lodge – an off-grid sanctuary that’s been recently renovated under new ownership. Five private log cabins combine timber interiors, wood-burning stoves and refined touches including wool throws, floor-to-ceiling windows and ambient lighting. The main lodge, where a chef prepares three meals per day for guests, has all the creature comforts of a cosy lounge, fireplace, wide viewing decks and outdoor hot tub. It's the hub for gathering with fellow travel companions and quiet relaxation. Days can be spent snowshoeing, skating or exploring trails by snowmobile. When night falls, head outside (or peer from your window) as the green and violet of the Aurora drift overhead. So you don't miss the experience, the lodge provides a door-knocking service to wake guests when the Aurora is shining.

Just outside Yellowknife, a heated dome glows softly amid the snow at North of 60 Aurora Adventures, a First Nations-owned, family-run operator that blends Aurora viewing with Dene culture. Inside the dome, a wood stove radiates warmth while curved windows offer a panoramic view to the celestial light show.

During the day, ride through open country with an experienced musher or take the reins yourself and feel the rush as your team surges forward and the dogsled skims fast and low over the powdery ground. During a Dene cultural session you’ll hear stories of a family shaped by generations of life on the land, try traditional instruments or axe throwing and dine on hearty stews as the afternoon light fades.

Soak in the spirit of the Yukon

false

original

The heart of Canada’s wild north, the Yukon is a place of soaring mountains, braided rivers and communities grounded in First Nations resilience and frontier spirit. It’s considered one of the world’s most dependable places to see the Aurora, with many immersive ways to experience it.

On Wild Adventure Yukon’s Romance Under the Aurora tour, you’ll journey south from Whitehorse along the Klondike Highway, winding through mountain valleys to a quiet clearing near Carcross. Chase the northern lights the traditional way, gliding through the wilderness on a dog sled. Then settle into a semi-private dome with a windowed roof to watch the lights shimmer while dining on charcuterie, a hearty chilli dinner and hot chocolate.

Take an aurora adventure with Northern Tales during a range of tour options that last from one to six nights. Depart from its base – just a 25-minute drive outside of Whitehorse – or arrange to be picked up directly from your hotel. Stay in a heated cabin or wall tent in an area renowned for spectacular visibility as part of its basic Aurora Borealis package; or combine this experience with a three-night stay in a waterfront cabin at Southern Lakes Resort in Whitehorse.

To embrace the Yukon spirit, Up North Adventures pairs snowshoeing or snowmobiling with a guided day of ice fishing. You’ll cross open country to a remote frozen lake, the air rich with woodsmoke from the crackling fire and crisp with the Arctic’s chill, drill through the ice’s glassy surface and drop a line below for a thrilling fishing adventure. For an unforgettable experience, North Country Yukon takes guests ice fishing at night, under the light of the Aurora.

Our top planning tips

  • If possible, book your domestic flight as a part of your international ticket. Qantas flies direct to Vancouver and codeshares with WestJet, which connects via Calgary (YYC) to Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Winnipeg. If you’re booking a tour, check with your operator for recommended flight connections.
  • Try to schedule your Aurora experience at the start or middle of your itinerary rather than the end to avoid possible weather or flight delays.

When to see the Northern Lights in Canada

  • Churchill, Manitoba: Best seen from January to early May and between late August and November. Autumn Aurora also gives you the chance to view the lights and polar bears on the same trip.
  • Northwest Territories and the Yukon: Best seen between mid August and November, when nights are longer.
